pages.name: Twelve cells
pages.task: A bank of 12 cells floats at 2.25 V a cell. What does the charger read?
pages.why: Cells in series add their volts. So the charger holds 12 × 2.25 = 27.00 V. That sits above the bank's rested 12 × 2.1 = 25.20 V, so a small current flows in.

pages.name: A charge from flat
pages.text: A flat 100 Ah battery charges in three stages. In [[bulk]] the charger holds 10 A, and the volts per cell climb. At 2.35 V a cell, inside the boost band, it holds the volts instead. That is [[topping]]. The current now falls by itself, because less sulphate is left to turn back. At 3 to 5 A the cell is full, and the charger drops to [[float]] at 2.25 V a cell.

pages.name: Is it full?
pages.task: On this 100 Ah battery the topping current has fallen from 10 A. It now holds at 4 A. Is the battery charged?
pages.answer: Yes: 4 A is 4 per cent of 100 Ah
pages.why: A cell counts as full when the topping current falls to 3 to 5 per cent of its Ah rating. On 100 Ah that is 3 to 5 A, and 4 A sits inside it. A full cell held at the charge setting still takes a little current, so it never reaches 0 A. Here the charger drops to float.

pages.name: Times the cells
pages.text: The float band belongs to one cell's chemistry, and cells in series add their volts. So you set one cell's figure and multiply by the cells. Here each cell floats at 2.23 V. Six cells need 13.38 V and twelve need 26.76 V. So 24 cells need 2.23 × 24 = 53.52 V.

pages.name: 55 cells
pages.task: A battery of 55 cells floats at 2.23 V a cell. What do you set the charger to?
pages.why: Multiply the float per cell by the number of cells: 2.23 × 55 = 122.65 V. The rested 2.1 V a cell gives 115.50 V, which would push almost nothing in. The nominal 2 V a cell gives 110.00 V, below the battery's own voltage.

pages.name: Too low, too high
pages.text: Two meters show what months at a set point do to the plates. Held at 2.15 V a cell, the cells never quite get back to full. [[Sulphate]] builds on the negative plate. Held at 2.45 V, current keeps flowing into a full cell. It thins the positive plate's grid. Past 2.40 V the cells also gas, and the water falls. So higher is not better. Back at 2.25 V, every meter stands still.

pages.name: Raised float
pages.task: Someone raises this bank's float from 2.25 V to 2.35 V a cell, to keep it fuller. What does a year of that do?
pages.answer: The positive grid corrodes faster, and the cells run warmer
pages.why: A full cell cannot store any more charge. At 2.35 V a cell it still takes more current than self-discharge needs. That current turns to heat, and it works on the positive grid, which corrodes. So the cells run warmer and the grid thins.

pages.name: Boost, then equalise
pages.text: A [[boost]] is a spell above float that refills the cells faster. The topping stage at 2.35 V was one. Here the charger boosts at 2.38 V a cell. The dashed trace stays at float the whole way, and fills later. At full the charger must drop back to float. An [[equalise]] is a deliberate overcharge at 2.50 V a cell, for a while. It clears built-up sulphate and levels the cells, and every cell gasses. Then the charger returns to float.

pages.name: Left on boost
pages.task: Friday's discharge was recharged on boost at 2.40 V a cell. On Monday the charger is still on boost. What has the weekend done?
pages.answer: Extra grid corrosion, and water lost as gas
pages.why: Boost is for recharging. Once the battery was full, 2.40 V a cell kept pushing current in. A full cell cannot store it. So it went to heat, to gas that carried water off, and to extra corrosion of the positive grid. Boost must go back to float at full.

pages.name: Warm cells
pages.text: Temperature moves the band too. A warm cell reacts more readily, so the same volts push more current in. So it needs a lower setting. A typical correction takes 3 mV a cell off for each degree above 25 °C. It adds 3 mV a cell for each degree below. These 24 cells float at 2.25 V a cell at 25 °C, which is 54.00 V. At 35 °C that falls to 2.22 V a cell, or 53.28 V.

pages.name: A cold room
pages.task: These cells float at 2.25 V a cell at 25 °C. The setting moves 3 mV a cell for each degree away from 25 °C. The cells sit at 15 °C. What float do you set?
pages.why: Colder needs a higher setting. 15 °C is 10 degrees below 25 °C. At 3 mV a cell for each degree, that is 30 mV, or 0.03 V. So set 2.25 + 0.03 = 2.28 V a cell.

pages.name: A year at 51.60 V
pages.task: A 24-cell charger has sat at 51.60 V for a year. What has that done?
pages.answer: Sulphate building on the negative plates
pages.why: Divide by the cells: 51.60 ÷ 24 = 2.15 V a cell. That is below the float band, so the cells never quite get back to full. The sulphate left on the negative plates builds up. Being above the rested 2.1 V only means a little current flows.

pages.name: Drifted cells
pages.task: After months on float, the specific gravities of this 24-cell battery have drifted apart. What does it need?
pages.answer: An equalise at 2.50 V a cell, 60.00 V, then back to float
pages.why: An equalise is a deliberate overcharge at 2.50 V a cell, for a while. On 24 cells that is 2.50 × 24 = 60.00 V. It clears built-up sulphate and brings the cells level. Then the charger goes back to float. Left on, it would corrode the grids and split water off as gas.

pages.name: Putting it back
pages.task: A DC supply charges this battery, positive to positive, through a resistor and an ammeter. The battery gave out 50 Ah. About how many ampere-hours must the supply put back?
pages.why: Some of the charge splits water into gas instead of filling the plates. So you put back about 1.2 times what came out: 50 × 1.2 = 60 Ah. Put the other way, 50 ÷ 60 is about 0.83, so about 83 per cent comes back. The supply sits above the battery's voltage, positive to positive, so current flows in. The resistor limits that current, and the ammeter shows it.
